job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Karl Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Karl, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my mum and my younger brother in a two-bedroom flat in Ridgemont, and I share a room with my brother, which is as fun as it sounds. Mornings I apply for jobs and polish my CV, afternoons I do a course online, and on Saturdays and Sundays I load parcels at the Eastgate distribution warehouse for a small wage. My mum cleans offices and her pay barely covers the rent, so she can't give me money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and how has the job search gone so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a business administration degree with a marketing option at Ridgemont College and passed with an average grade. My final project was a marketing plan for a local bakery called Hollis Bakes, and the owner actually used two of my ideas. I've applied for about forty roles in nine months, mostly marketing assistant and customer operations jobs, and I've had three interviews but no offer. I owe a lot in student loans and have maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably oversold, but still worth keeping an eye on. At the warehouse, the guys joke that it's just another app, and I'd agree. Online I'd stay quiet, because I'm not an expert, and I'd rather see proof first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my own situation doesn't get better or worse because of AI. The problem is still too many graduates and too few starter jobs in Ridgemont. I'd rather there were a boom, even a hyped one, because hype creates hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with forty applications every quarter, and add the customer service and logistics firms near the Eastgate depot, since I already know people there. I'd finish the free data analytics course I'm halfway through, which takes about three more months. I'd also ask the warehouse supervisor, Mr Okafor, about a full-time contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, to be honest. It's the same grind, just without a deadline. I'm not scared, but I'm not hopeful either, and I get tired of explaining to relatives that no, I still haven't got a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for, and would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use ChatGPT sometimes to tidy a cover letter or practise interview questions. It's useful, not magic, and every other applicant does it too, so it doesn't make me stand out. In this picture I'd keep using it the same way, which is occasionally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about the next year, even if AI changes little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan payments start growing once I earn above the threshold, and I'm not even there yet. And my mum's rent goes up every year. If my brother's school costs rise, I'd be the one expected to help, even though I have nothing to give.

say: I'd say AI is probably **oversold**, but I'd want proof before saying more.
I'd tell friends that **hype** still creates hiring.
think: My problem is too many graduates and too few **starter jobs** in Ridgemont.
The flat feeling worries me more than any technology: the same **grind** with no deadline.
do: Keep applying, adding **customer service and logistics** firms near the Eastgate depot.
Finish the free data analytics course in about three months.
Ask Mr Okafor, my warehouse supervisor, about a full-time contract.
feel: A bit **flat**: the same grind, not scared but not hopeful.
S0.quote: I'm not scared, but I'm not hopeful either, and I get tired of explaining to relatives that no, I still haven't got a job.
fieldNote: Pragmatic and sceptical; wants proof before speaking up.
The **debt** and his mother's rent matter more to him than AI in this picture.
His warehouse weekend job is a real, practical route to a contract.

steps.text: Apply to customer service and logistics firms near the depot
Finish the free data analytics course in three months
Ask the warehouse supervisor about a full-time contract
Keep sending a few applications every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what regulation is for. If firms use software to cut staff, they should have to show where the savings go. At the warehouse we'd push the union to ask for retraining before anyone gets laid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the first-job marketing and customer roles I'm applying for are exactly the thinking tasks that go first. Writing posts, scheduling, answering customer emails, building reports, that's most of an entry job. Employers will say they need one junior instead of four, and I'm one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop sending the same CV everywhere and learn what the tools can do, so I can say I run them rather than compete with them. I'd finish the analytics course and add a short course on marketing automation. And I'd ask Hollis Bakes whether I could run their social posts and email list for a small fee, as proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's some energy in it. It scares me that I'm at the very start when the ground moves, but being young means I can adapt if someone gives me a path. I'd rather be told straight than be reassured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a marketing or operations entry job do you think move to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scheduling social posts, writing product descriptions, sorting leads, making weekly reports, and answering simple customer chats. Those are what my cousin did in his first marketing job, and his firm replaced two of them with software last spring. I know this because he told me over dinner, a bit ashamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government or employers if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a training fund that firms pay into, and I'd want paid placements instead of free internships. At the very least, a guaranteed interview for graduates who finish a retraining course. Otherwise the loan stays and the entry job doesn't.

feel: Worried, with some **energy**: scared at the start, but able to adapt.

Wants a fair deal from firms through regulation and training funds.

steps.text: Finish the analytics course and add a marketing automation course
Offer Hollis Bakes a paid trial running their social posts
Ask the warehouse union to press for retraining before layoffs
Write to my MP asking for a graduate training fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency measures, something like income support and a pause on loan payments. Two years is far too fast for firms or families. I'd get on the phone to my union rep and say we have to prepare the warehouse workers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. The whole desk job market I trained for would be gone before I've even had one job, and my mum's cleaning work is safer for now, which is a strange thing to say. I'd feel like I picked the wrong decade to be twenty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with my mum and list every bill. Then I'd ask Mr Okafor for as many warehouse shifts as he can give me, since robots take three more years to arrive. I'd also stop the online course and put the time into any paid trial work, plus an application a day to anything with a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and a bit numb. I'd try to look calm for my mum, but at night I'd run the numbers over and over, and they don't work. It feels like the floor tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands-on warehouse work should last until about 2031, so I'd treat those shifts as my lifeline. I'd learn the scanners and the forklift licence, which cost about two hundred pounds. It's not what I studied for, but at least it's a job that still exists in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would be hit hardest, and how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, because she's the only steady wage and the rent depends on it. If I can't contribute, she'd skip meals before she'd ask for help. My brother would feel it in school, because his trips and uniform would be the first things cut.

say: I'd call for **emergency income support** and a pause on loan payments.
I'd tell my union rep the warehouse workers need preparing too.
think: The desk jobs I trained for would be gone before I've had one, so I picked the **wrong decade**.
The warehouse is a lifeline because **hands-on work** lasts about three years longer.
do: List every household bill with my mum in the first week.
Ask for as many **warehouse shifts** as I can get.
Pay about two hundred pounds for a forklift licence.
feel: **Frightened** and numb, running the numbers each night and finding they don't work.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I picked the wrong decade to be twenty-three.
fieldNote: Moves from white-collar hopes to **hands-on** warehouse shifts as a bridge.
His family worry centres on his mother and younger brother.
Plans are specific: shifts, licence and the family budget.

steps.text: Ask for as many warehouse shifts as possible
Pay for a forklift licence for about two hundred pounds
List every household bill and cut the extras with my mum
Ask the union rep about emergency hardship help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to organise something fair, so we should start now. I'd tell friends to learn what they can and not wait. And I'd back any plan that makes firms contribute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get a few working years if I move fast, but the entry-level job ladder in business would be gone by the end. So I'd want to be in something AI adjacent or people facing by then. I can't stay a junior marketing assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid role in customer operations or logistics office work to get started, even at low pay. I'd put aside fifty pounds a month, the analytics certificate would be done in the first year, and I'd start offering small marketing services to local shops. I'd also keep the warehouse weekends going for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years, but still heavy. It's a bit like knowing a storm is coming and having time to board up some windows, but not all of them. I'd feel more in control, which counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not the forklift licence straight away. With five years I'd look at the data course and small client work first, since they build skills that count after 2031. The licence stays as a backup if things go badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still pay for a forklift licence in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means being able to try one plan and, if it fails, try another. In two years I only get one go. In five I could take a job, learn on it, fail at it, and still have time to move. That is the main difference for me.

say: I'd say five years is enough to organise something fair, so start now.
I'd back any plan making firms **contribute**.
think: I'd get a few working years if I move fast, but the **entry ladder** would be gone by the end.

feel: More in **control** than with two years, but still heavy.

fieldNote: The longer warning changes his plan from survival to **trial and adjustment**.

steps.text: Take any paid customer operations or logistics office job
Put aside fifty pounds a month

Finish the analytics certificate within the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we don't waste it. I'd push for schools and colleges to teach how to work with AI, and I'd say firms must train juniors. I'd be fairly relaxed online, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have a real chance, because ten years is long enough to build a career, even if it's in something else. I'd be thirty-three by 2036, and I'd want to be the person who runs the tools in a small firm. The debt is still a worry, but it's one I can pay down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any first job now and build skills beside it. I'd finish the analytics certificate and then try a part-time master's, maybe in data or operations, if a firm pays part of it. I'd also save a hundred pounds a month and pay the loan down faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a bit of excitement. It's the first scenario where I feel I could plan a life, like maybe renting my own place and helping my mum. I'd still have bad days when the applications don't land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do differently about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do a degree that mixes business and data, not pure marketing. Marketing is the part that software takes first. But at the time I picked it because I liked the bakery project, and I don't regret that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother, Danny, to get a skill with people or hands in it, and to treat AI like a tool he learns early. I'd say don't take on loans for a degree just because everyone expects it. And I'd tell him I'm proud of him for working hard at school.

Finish the analytics certificate, then try a **part-time master's** if a firm pays part.

S4.quote: I'd be thirty-three by 2036, and I'd want to be the person who runs the tools in a small firm.
fieldNote: With a decade he plans a **career** rather than a survival route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because I'd have the least time and no cushion. What would help is a pause on loan payments, paid training with a guaranteed interview, and honest advice about which jobs will last. Also firms that give juniors a real chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me, with an average degree, aren't asking for a handout. We want a fair start. If the entry jobs shrink, we need a bridge, and I'd like someone in charge to say that out loud.

headlineQuote: People like me, with an average degree, aren't asking for a handout. We want a fair start.
portrait: Karl (23) lives with his mum and brother in **Ridgemont**, owes student loans and has about three weeks of savings.
He holds a pass in business administration with a marketing option and has had three interviews from forty applications.
He loads parcels at a warehouse at weekends and uses **AI tools** now and then.
He is practical and fair-minded, wanting **regulation** and training funds but also acting for himself.
He moves from survival in the fast scenarios to a real career plan when there are ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because there'd be the least time and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan payment pause**, paid training with a guaranteed interview and honest advice on lasting jobs.
